text: ArgoCD and Flux both just point at a path in a repo — neither one tells you how to organize that repo across dev, staging, and prod. That's a structural decision you make once, early, and live with for a long time, and there are three shapes most teams reach for.

Directory-per-environment keeps one repo with a base directory holding environment-agnostic manifests, plus one overlay folder per environment that patches only what differs. Branch-per-environment instead tracks dev, staging, and main as separate branches, where promotion means merging one forward into the next. Repo-per-environment goes further still, sometimes forking the whole config repo, more often splitting application source into one repo and deployable config into a separate one entirely.

The Kustomize version of directory-per-environment looks like this: a base folder with the shared deployment and service manifests, and an overlays folder with one subdirectory per environment, each one only overriding what's actually different — replica count, resource limits, the image tag.

A staging overlay's kustomization-dot-yaml references the base as its resources, applies a replica patch, and sets the image tag to the version being promoted. Because the only thing changing is often that one newTag line, promoting a build from one environment to the next can be a single-line diff in a pull request — easy to review, easy to revert.

Each pattern trades something real. Directories give you the best side-by-side visibility — one git diff shows every environment at once — but access control is coarser unless you add branch protection or CODEOWNERS rules per path. Branches feel familiar if your team already thinks in GitFlow terms, but comparing environments means diffing branches instead of folders, and a hotfix to main can drift ahead of staging without anyone noticing. Separate repos give the strongest isolation and audit trail, at the cost of more repos and more cross-repo automation to keep them in sync.

Most real ArgoCD and Flux setups land on directories with Kustomize overlays in one config repo, often paired with a separate app-source repo just for the build step. Next lesson puts that structure to work in a concrete promotion workflow — moving one validated build from dev to staging to production without ever rebuilding it along the way.
